pride_data.title: PLAA/UFD-3 regulates P-bodies through its intrinsic disordered domain
pride_data.projectDescription: global proteomics analysis for ufd3 knock out C. elegans and wild type, ubiquitin enrichment analysis for ufd3 knock-out and wild type in C. elegans; proximity labeling analysis(TurboID) for ufd3 knock-out and wild type in C. elegans.
pride_data.sampleProcessingProtocol: LC-MS/MS analysis of the digested peptides were performed on an EASY-nLC 1200 (Thermo Fisher Scientific) coupled to an Orbitrap Eclipse Tribrid mass spectrometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific). Peptides were separated on an Aurora UHPLC column (25 cm × 75 µm, 1.6 µm C18, AUR2-25075C18A, Ion Opticks) with a flow rate of 0.35 µL/min for a total duration of 196 min ionized at 1.6 kV in the positive ion mode. The gradient was composed of 6% solvent B (11 min), 6-25% B (124 min), 25-40% B (45 min), 40–98% B (1 min) and 98% B (15min); solvent A: 2% ACN and 0.2% FA in water; solvent B: 80% ACN and 0.2% FA. MS1 scans were acquired at the resolution of 120,000 from 375 to 2,000 m/z, AGC target 1e6, and maximum injection time 50 ms. MS2 scans were acquired in the ion trap using fast scan rate on precursors with 2-7 charge states and quadrupole isolation mode (isolation window: 0.7 m/z) with higher-energy collisional dissociation (HCD, 30%) activation type. Dynamic exclusion was set to 30 s. The temperature of ion transfer tube was 300°C and the S-lens RF level was set to 30.
pride_data.dataProcessingProtocol: Raw data files were analyzed using Proteome Discoverer (PD) (version 3.0, Thermo Fisher Scientific) based on the CHIMERYS algorithm against in silico tryptic digested Uniprot C. elegans reference proteome database. The maximum missed cleavages were set to 2. Dynamic modifications were set to oxidation on methionine (M, +15.995 Da) and carbamidomethylation on cysteine residues (C, +57.021 Da) was set as a fixed modification. The maximum parental mass error was set to 10 ppm, and the MS2 mass tolerance was set to 0.3 Da. The false discovery threshold was set strictly to 0.01 using the Percolator Node validated by q-value. The relative abundance of parental peptides was calculated by integration of the area under the curve of the MS1 peaks using the Minora LFQ node.

passages.text: PLAA/UFD-3 regulates P-bodies through its intrinsic disordered domain
Significance

Phospholipase A2 activating protein (PLAA) is implicated in a set of neurodevelopmental disorders such as lethal infantile epileptic encephalopathy, autism and neurodevelopmental disorder with progressive microcephaly, spasticity, and brain anomalies (NDMSBA). It plays a central role in ubiquitin-dependent protein degradation via its strong ubiquitin binding and/or interaction with valosin-containing protein (VCP/p97). In this study, we uncovered an interaction between the Caenorhabditis elegans PLAA ortholog ubiquitin fusion degradation 3 (UFD-3) and a regulatory subunit of the mRNA decapping complex (DCAP-1). We showed that the UFD-3 intrinsic disordered domain, containing conserved motifs, is critical for this interaction, but is not required for ubiquitin-dependent protein degradation. Our findings link UFD-3 to two major hubs of proteome regulation, translation, and degradation.

Regulation of proteome homeostasis is crucial for the survival and adaptation to changing environments for all species. In eukaryotes, this process is finely tuned through regulation at the level of transcription, translation, protein modification, and protein degradation. The phospholipase A2 activating protein (PLAA) is present in all eukaryotes and believed to be a key player in ubiquitin-dependent protein sorting and degradation via its interactions with ubiquitin and/or the AAA+ ATPase, valosin-containing protein (VCP/p97). PLAA’s molecular targets and interaction network remain unclear. We used Caenorhabditis elegans and unbiased proteome-scale approaches to investigate neuronal specific interactors of the C. elegans PLAA ortholog UFD-3 (ubiquitin fusion degradation 3), its effect on ubiquitinated proteins, and global protein expression changes in an ufd-3 mutant. We found that PLAA may play a unique role in cytoplasmic messenger ribonucleic acid (mRNA) processing bodies (P-bodies). Using biochemical analysis in vitro and fluorescence imaging in C. elegans, we show that UFD-3 directly interacts with the mRNA decapping complex regulatory subunit DCAP-1. UFD-3's intrinsic disordered region (IDR), which contains conserved amino acid motifs, is important for the recruitment of DCAP-1 to P-bodies. Finally, we show that loss of the IDR does not affect UFD-3's role in sorting ubiquitinated proteins through the multivesicular body pathway. Collectively, our results suggest that UFD-3's role in P-bodies is distinct from its role in the ubiquitin-dependent protein degradation pathway and the IDR is only critical for UFD-3-regulated P-bodies pathways. Thus, PLAA/UFD-3 might regulate the proteome via two distinct pathways: ubiquitinated protein turnover, as well as mRNA regulation through P-bodies.

Cellular homeostasis and adaptive responses to shifting environments depend on the balance of gene expression, posttranscriptional control, posttranslational modifications, and protein turnover. Gene expression controls the production of RNA transcripts, setting the foundation for protein synthesis. Posttranscriptional regulation, including splicing and 5′ and 3′ end modifications, controls mRNA stability and rate of translation, allowing cells to fine-tune protein levels on a faster time scale than transcription. Once proteins are synthesized, posttranslational modifications such as phosphorylation, ubiquitination, and acetylation further adjust protein activity, stability, cellular localization, and interaction networks, enabling rapid cellular responses to change in their environment. Protein turnover, governed by mechanisms including the ubiquitin–proteasome degradation and autophagy-mediated degradation pathways, removes proteins that are damaged or are no longer needed, thus preventing their accumulation and ensuring proteome integrity. This continuous cycle of synthesis, modification, and degradation allows cells to adapt dynamically, balancing stability with flexibility to meet metabolic and developmental demands while minimizing errors and cellular stress.

Phospholipase A2 activating protein (PLAA) plays an important role in regulating protein turnover in multiple cellular pathways. As its name suggests, PLAA was first discovered as an activator of Phospholipase A2. Although the molecular mechanism of Phospholipase A2 activation by PLAA is unclear, cell biology studies have shown PLAA to play roles in the ubiquitin-mediated protein degradation pathway, sorting of proteins into multivesicular bodies, clearance of ruptured lysosomes by autophagy, and stress granule formation. Human genetic studies implicate PLAA in lethal infantile epileptic encephalopathy, neurodevelopmental disorder with progressive microcephaly, spasticity, and brain anomalies (NDMSBA), and autism spectrum disorder. PLAA has also been shown to suppress ovarian cancer metastasis via METTL3-mediated modification of the mRNA encoding transient receptor potential channel canonical-3 (TRPC3).

PLAA is a multidomain protein whose overall domain architecture (Fig. 1A) is conserved in all eukaryotes. At its amino-terminus, PLAA contains a WD40 domain that binds ubiquitin with a Kd of ~220 μM for monoubiquitin and Kd of ~40 μM for linear di-ubiquitin. The central PFU (PLAA family ubiquitin-binding) domain is unique to PLAA family proteins and has no homology to other known ubiquitin-binding domains. Although the PFU domain has been shown to be able to bind ubiquitin, albeit with a much lower affinity than the WD40 domain (Kd of ~1 mM), it is not clear whether this interaction is relevant in vivo. In the budding yeast, Saccharomyces cerevisiae, binding of the PFU domain of the PLAA homolog Doa1p to the SH3 domain of STAM homolog Hse1 is important for sorting proteins to multivesicular bodies. The C-terminal PUL (PLAP, UFD3, and lub1) domain is an alpha-helical globular domain that mediates protein–protein interactions. Notably, the PUL domain is the binding site for the AAA+ ATPase valosin-containing protein (VCP)/p97, a prominent AAA+ ATPase.

PLAA contains an intrinsically disordered region (IDR) connecting the PFU and PUL domains as inferred from unstructured regions in published crystal structures [PDB ID: 3L3F, PDB ID: 3PSP]. IDRs confer conformational flexibility, are often the sites of posttranslational modifications, and allow for multiple types of protein interactions and tethering to promote multiplex formation. Many proteins with large IDRs can spontaneously undergo liquid–liquid phase separation (LLPS) under physiological conditions, leading to the formation of intracellular condensates, characterized by a dense network of multivalent weak interactions between proteins and/or RNA. Several types of such ribonucleoprotein (RNP) granules are reported in neurons including processing bodies (P-bodies), stress granules, transport RNPs, translation complex, and RNA-induced silencing complex (RISC). These different types of RNP granules can be distinguished by their composition, location, and function. P-bodies are a type of cytoplasmic ribonucleoprotein condensate, where mRNAs are stored in a translationally inactive but stable form, and can be dynamically released to control their spatiotemporal distribution and translation. The enzymes DCP1 (mRNA-decapping enzyme 1) and DCP2 (mRNA-decapping enzyme 2) are central to RNA regulation in the P-bodies. In RNA homeostasis, DCP2 is responsible for catalyzing the removal of the 5′ 7-methylguanosine cap to inhibit translation. DCP1 is the decapping complex regulatory subunit that has dynamic roles in stabilizing DCP2 and recruiting the decapping coactivators EDC3 (enhancer of mRNA-decapping protein 3) and EDC4 (enhancer of mRNA-decapping protein 4).

Although many of PLAA’s functions depend on its association with VCP and VCP-cofactors, a study in yeast suggested that PLAA performs some functions that are independent of its association with VCP. PLAA’s interaction with its molecular targets, and how PLAA may function in pathways other than ubiquitin-mediated protein degradation is not well understood. Here, we prioritized a proteomics-based approach to identify interactors of PLAA and used Caenorhabditis elegans for analyzing cellular phenotypes in the context of an intact organism. We used genome editing to mutate ufd-3, the C. elegans ortholog of PLAA, and characterized the phenotypic consequences of loss of ufd-3 function. We performed proteomic analyses to identify neuron-specific UFD-3 interactors using TurboID proximity labeling and defined UFD-3-dependent ubiquitinated proteins to identify cellular pathways influenced by UFD-3. Both analyses pointed to P-bodies. We found that UFD-3 interacts with the critical P-body component DCAP-1. Finally, we showed that the UFD-3 IDR is important for DCAP-1 recruitment to P-bodies but not for sorting and degradation of ubiquitinated proteins.
Results
ufd-3 Null Mutant Worms Have Growth, Locomotory, and Sensory Defects.

We created three different ufd-3 knockout (KO) alleles using CRISPR. We inserted a STOP-IN cassette within the coding region in the 5’ exons of the two different isoforms (sy1796 and sy1798, Fig. 1B, see SI Appendix, Table S1). We also deleted the entire coding sequence using CRISPR (sy2087, Fig. 1B, see SI Appendix, Table S1). In all three cases, the ufd-3 KO worms grew slower than control worms (Fig. 1C). The ufd-3 KO worms also had brood sizes less than half those of wild-type worms (Fig. 1D). Since variants in PLAA have been linked to neurodevelopmental disorders in humans, we next tested whether ufd-3 KO worms had any defects in neuron development or had motor or sensory impairment. There were no obvious differences in PVD dendrite arborization at the L4 stage between control and ufd-3 KO worms (SI Appendix, Fig. S1). ufd-3 KO worms explored a much smaller area and moved at a slower speed compared to control worms (Fig. 1 E and F). ufd-3 KO worms were defective in chemotaxis toward the volatile compounds, benzaldehyde and diacetyl (Fig. 1G). ufd-3 KO males also showed defects in multiple aspects of mating behavior, starting with a defect in responding to hermaphrodite contact (Fig. 1H). The adult lifespan of ufd-3 KO worms was shorter than that of wild-type worms, with median values of 12 d and 14 d, respectively (Fig. 1I).
Proteomic Analysis Reveals UFD-3's Involvement in P-Bodies.

To understand the basis of these developmental and behavioral defects, we turned to proteomic approaches. We first used label-free whole animal proteomics to identify differentially expressed proteins between control and ufd-3 KO animals. For this experiment, we prepared lysates of the control and the two UFD-3 STOP-IN mutant strains and analyzed their protein expression level by liquid chromatography–tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS). Of the >6,500 detected proteins, 1,099 proteins were differentially expressed (fold-change > 2 or fold-change < 0.5, P-value < 0.05) in at least one of the two ufd-3 KO strains compared to the wild type (Fig. 2A, see SI Appendix, Fig. S2 A and B). 183 and 133 proteins were detected at twofold lower or higher levels, respectively, in both ufd-3 KO genotypes compared to control (Fig. 2 B, pink dots in Upper-Right and Lower-Left Quadrants).

Previous studies showed that UFD-3 regulated ubiquitin fusion degradation pathway. GFP tagged with noncleavable ubiquitin (ubiquitin-G76V) accumulated in ufd-3 mutants in Saccharomyces cerevisiae and in C. elegans, indicating that UFD-3 can promote the degradation of ubiquitin-tagged proteins. To identify the ubiquitinated protein targets of UFD-3, we immunoprecipitated peptides containing the ubiquitin remnant motif (K-ε-GG) from trypsin-digested control and ufd-3 KO (sy2087) worm lysates. We analyzed these peptides using quantitative mass spectroscopy and compared fold-changes of identified proteins between wild-type and ufd-3 KO. Of the 3,261 proteins identified in the ubiquitin enrichment experiment, 91 were significantly enriched (fold-change > 2, P-value < 0.05) in the ufd-3 KO strain compared to the wild type (SI Appendix, Fig. S2C and Dataset S2). These 91 proteins are potential targets of UFD-3 and we refer to this set of 91 proteins as the “UFD-3 ubiquitome.” For a majority of these 91 proteins, total protein levels were not significantly altered between wild-type and ufd-3 KO strains, and only 13 of these 91 proteins were found at significantly higher or lower levels, in at least one of the two ufd-3 KO strains compared to the wild type (SI Appendix, Fig. S2D).

To identify a neuron-specific UFD-3 interactome, we conducted a neuron-specific proximity labeling assay. We created a strain expressing TurboID fused with UFD-3 in neuronal cells. We enriched the worm lysates for biotinylated proteins and analyzed the composition of the extract using quantitative mass spectroscopy. We performed the experiment for three types of samples: i) control worms not expressing TurboID::UFD-3 (AX7884), fed with biotin-rich bacteria; ii) worms expressing TurboID::UFD-3, fed with biotin-rich bacteria; and iii) worms expressing TurboID::UFD-3, fed with biotin-deficient bacteria as a more stringent control. We detected a total of 4,813 proteins across all three samples. To identify UFD-3 interacting proteins with high accuracy, we compared the levels of each protein in test vs. two control conditions and selected the candidates that passed our threshold criteria (fold-change > 4 and P-value < 0.05) (SI Appendix, Fig. S2 E and F). Using these criteria, we found 1,429 proteins that were enriched in samples expressing TurboID::UFD-3 vs. wild type (Fig. 2C, see SI Appendix, Fig. S2E), and 1,653 proteins that were enriched in TurboID::UFD-3 expressing samples fed with biotin-rich vs. biotin-deficient bacteria (Fig. 2C, see SI Appendix, Fig. S2F). 983 proteins were enriched in both sets (Fig. 2C and Dataset S3), although the fold-changes of these proteins were only weakly correlated between the two sets (Fig. 2D). These proteins are potential UFD-3 interactors and we refer to this set of 983 proteins as the “UFD-3 interactome.”

We performed Gene Ontology term enrichment analyses with the UFD-3 ubiquitome and UFD-3 interactome sets. GO terms related to the vesicle transport system were enriched among the proteins in both sets (SI Appendix, Tables S2 and S3). Our analyses also revealed the enrichment of proteins associated with mRNA processing pathways and more specifically, P-bodies, in both UFD-3 interactor and UFD-3 effector sets (SI Appendix, Tables S2 and S3). 35 C. elegans proteins are annotated with the GO term, P-body (GO:0000932). For four of these 35 proteins, fold-changes could not be calculated in any of our proteomic experiments (Fig. 2E). Most of the remaining 31 P-body proteins did not show significant differential expression between control and ufd-3 KO samples (exception: LIN-41) (Fig. 2E). We observed enriched accumulation of ubiquitinated LSM-1, CCF-1, and RPB-7 in ufd-3 KO animals compared to the wild type (Fig. 2E). In the neuron-specific TurboID experiment, we observed strong enrichment of several P-body proteins including DCAP-1, LSM-4, PATR-1, and RDE-12 (Fig. 2E). Collectively, our proteomic data indicate that UFD-3 may play a role in P-body regulation and function.
UFD-3 Recruits DCAP-1 to P-Bodies through Its IDR Domain.

We next explored UFD-3's role in P-bodies in living C. elegans animals. Since P-bodies are ribonucleoprotein condensates formed by LLPS, and disordered regions in proteins are often a major driving factor for phase separation, we asked whether UFD-3's IDR domain is important for its role in P-bodies. The UFD-3 IDR domain contains three conserved motifs (Fig. 3A, orange), while the sequence outside of these motifs has low complexity. The first five amino acids of this motif [DP(F/Y/W/L)TGxxxYxx] are highly conserved, while the latter half contains a conserved tyrosine residue at the 9th position (Fig. 3 A, Top). This motif is unique to the PLAA family proteins and most multicellular eukaryotic species, including C. elegans, have at least one copy of this motif in the IDR of a PLAA orthologous protein. These conserved sequences are notably absent in some unicellular eukaryotes, including the ciliate Paramecium primaurelia and the yeast S. cerevisiae, and are partially conserved in the biflagellated unicellular green algae, Chlamydomonas reinhardtii. Some vertebrates, including human, mouse, chicken, and Xenopus have multiple PLAA splice variants with variable numbers of this motif in the IDR (SI Appendix, Table S4). These observations suggest that this motif may play an important binding and/or regulatory role, and complex organisms have evolved ways to fine-tune this regulation by varying the number of motifs. Such evolution, thought to accelerate interactome adaptability, is one signature of eukaryotic short linear motifs (SLiMs).

To understand UFD-3’s role in P-bodies, we first asked whether loss of UFD-3 affected P-bodies in vivo. Given that DCAP-1 is widely used as a canonical P-body marker, and it is one of the most prominent hits in our UFD-3 interactor list, we used DCAP-1::dsRed to visualize P-bodies in living C. elegans animals. Since DCAP-1::dsRed fluorescence intensity increases with age of the worms, we synchronized our worm populations tightly by picking L4 stage worms 18 h before imaging. In control animals, punctate DCAP-1 signal was visible in several tissues, but was brightest in the head region (Fig. 3C). DCAP-1::dsRed signal was significantly dimmer in ufd-3 KO animals compared to control animals (Fig. 3 C and D). Since the formation and abundance of RNP condensates formed by LLPS is often sensitive to the local concentration of key components, we wondered whether the loss of UFD-3 shifted the equilibrium in favor of P-body disassembly. However, although the DCAP-1 signal was dimmer, we observed no major difference in the average abundance of P-bodies between control and ufd-3 KO animals (SI Appendix, Fig. S3 A–C). Additionally, we did not detect significant changes in DCAP-1 levels between control and ufd-3 KO animals in our mass spectroscopy data (Fig. 2E, dark and light pink). Thus, our data suggest that loss of UFD-3 reduces DCAP-1 recruitment to P-bodies without affecting P-body formation or stability.

We then asked whether the UFD-3 IDR is important for UFD-3's role in P-bodies. To test this, we used CRISPR-mediated genome editing to delete a portion of the IDR including the first two conserved motifs and the first five amino acids of the third motif (ΔIDR in Fig. 3 A and B). Using mass spectrometry, we first confirmed that the ufd-3 ΔIDR strain expressed the truncated UFD-3 protein. Contrary to the ufd-3 KO strain, ufd-3 ΔIDR animals did not exhibit any general health defects such as slow growth rate, low brood size, altered locomotion, lower lifespan, or defects in chemotaxis to volatile odors (SI Appendix, Fig. S3 D–I), indicating that the truncated protein was at least partially functional. Next, we observed DCAP-1::dsRed fluorescence in ufd-3 ΔIDR animals. We found that DCAP-1::dsRed fluorescence intensity was significantly reduced in ufd-3 ΔIDR animals compared to control, to the same extent as ufd-3 KO animals (Fig. 3D). Thus, our observations suggest that the conserved motifs in the UFD-3 IDR domain recruit DCAP-1 to P-bodies.

Another characteristic feature of SLiMs is their low affinity for binding partners, typically ranging from 1 to 150 μM, which enables reversible and transient interactions. To gain a deeper understanding of the interaction between UFD-3 and DCAP-1, we developed expression systems for both proteins. We fused them to His-tags for efficient purification using Ni-NTA affinity chromatography, followed by further purification through size exclusion chromatography (SEC) to ensure a high degree of purity (SI Appendix, Fig. S3 J and K). Once purification was complete, we quantitatively analyzed the interaction between UFD-3 and DCAP-1 using microscale thermophoresis (MST). We found that UFD-3 and DCAP-1 interacted with a dissociation constant (Kd) of 75.6 nM (Fig. 3E), indicating a rather strong interaction. Collectively, our results suggest that UFD-3 directly interacts with DCAP-1, possibly through its IDR domain and this interaction is necessary for DCAP-1 enrichment in P-bodies.
UFD-3 IDR Is Not Necessary for UFD-3’s Role in Ubiquitin-Dependent Protein Degradation Pathways.

Next, we asked whether the UFD-3 IDR domain is necessary for other functions of UFD-3, such as sorting ubiquitinated membrane proteins for degradation. Since ufd-3 KO males showed a defect in mating behavior, we investigated the localization and turnover of the male-specific transient receptor protein polycystin (TRPP) channel protein PKD-2, which was previously shown to be important for mating behavior. Other studies reported that PKD-2 levels in the cilia of male-specific sensory ray neurons are adjusted by regulation of their removal from cilia, internalization into endosomes at the ciliary base, and degradation through the lysosomal degradation pathway. In control animals, we observed PKD-2::GFP in the cilia and periciliary membrane compartments as reported in previous publications. For analysis, we focused on ray neurons R3b, R4b, and R5b, as these rays did not overlap with each other or with other structures in most of the samples. We observed a dramatically increased accumulation of PKD-2::GFP in the cilia and periciliary membrane compartments in the ufd-3 KO animals (Fig. 4 A, B, and D). This is likely because the loss of UFD-3 disrupts a critical step in sorting ubiquitinated endosomal proteins for degradation, leading to overaccumulation of PKD-2 within endosomes at the cilia base. However, the ufd-3 ΔIDR animals did not show the same defect, and the PKD-2 levels and distribution were similar to control animals (Fig. 4 A, C, and D). These results strongly suggest that the UFD-3 IDR domain is necessary for recruiting DCAP-1 to P-bodies, but not for ubiquitin-dependent protein degradation functions mediated by UFD-3.

Discussion

PLAA/UFD-3 family proteins have ubiquitin-binding domains and are known to be involved in ubiquitin recycling and ubiquitin-dependent protein degradation pathways. Previous studies have shown that ubiquitinated proteins accumulate in ufd-3 mutants (Fig. 5). However, studies in yeast have shown that this defect is linked to greatly reduced levels of free ubiquitin and is suppressed by ubiquitin overexpression. On the other hand, the S. cerevisiae PLAA ortholog Doa1p’s role in sorting ubiquitinated membrane proteins into multivesicular bodies (MVB) for vacuolar degradation, ribophagy, and in the DNA damage response by regulating monoubiquitination of histone H2B are independent of ubiquitin depletion. Many of PLAA/UFD-3 functions studied to date depend on its interactions with the conserved AAA+ ATPase VCP, which plays an essential role in many ubiquitin-dependent cellular processes central to protein quality control by segregating polyubiquitinated proteins from complexes or membranes, while Qiu et al. suggest that at least a subset of PLAA’s functions, including sorting of proteins along the MVB pathway, is not dependent upon interaction with VCP. To understand how PLAA/UFD-3 performs complex cellular roles in an intact animal, we generated and analyzed knockout mutations of ufd-3, which encodes the C. elegans ortholog of human PLAA and yeast Doa1p. After observing growth, fertility, sensorimotor, and longevity phenotypes of ufd-3 mutants, we used proteomic approaches in whole worms to identify targets and interactors of UFD-3.

Diagram showing PLAA/UFD-3’s roles in modulating the proteome through multiple pathways. Proteasomal degradation of soluble ubiquitinated proteins (teal) is inhibited in ufd-3 mutants. Cytoplasmic condensates formed by LLPS (P-body: red, stress granules: blue) and misfolded protein aggregates (polyQ: purple) are cleared by VCP-mediated autophagy in wild-type animals. In ufd-3 mutants, DCAP-1 recruitment to P-body is reduced and stress granules appear smaller and dispersed, leading to possibly altered translation. Fewer polyQ aggregates form in ufd-3 mutant animals. Transmembrane proteins (green), which are normally degraded though the MVB pathway in wild-type cells, accumulate within endosomes in the ufd-3 mutant.

We found an enrichment of P-body proteins in two distinct types of proteomic experiments, namely proximity labeling by TurboID::UFD-3 and differential levels of ubiquitinated proteins between control and ufd-3 KO samples. We then showed that UFD-3 controls the recruitment of the mRNA decapping complex protein DCAP-1 to P-bodies and the UFD-3 IDR domain is necessary for this process, despite being dispensable for other UFD-3 functions. Previous studies in human U2OS cells have shown that while the mRNA decapping complex catalytic subunit DCAP-2 is a nondynamic P-body core protein, the regulatory subunit, DCAP-1, rapidly exchanges with the cytoplasm. This indicates that DCAP-1 is loosely associated with P-bodies and local changes in the concentration of P-body-associated proteins can shift the equilibrium of DCAP-1 partitioning between soluble and condensate phases. IDRs in proteins often drive LLPS, enabling sequestration of biomolecules within membraneless mini-organelles, allowing for the efficient organization and localized execution of biochemical reactions. Commonly nested within IDRs are SLiMS, which have previously been shown to promote P-bodies through multivalent interactions in proteins such as the DCAP-2 coactivator EDC-3, enhancer of mRNA decapping 3. We showed that UFD-3/PLAA possesses highly conserved IDRs with SLiM-like architecture that potentially facilitate the multivalent interactions necessary for the formation of condensates during LLPS. Notably, DCAP-1 accumulation in P-bodies has been shown to increase dramatically in dcap-2 null mutant C. elegans, despite no change in dcap-1 mRNA levels, suggesting posttranscriptional regulation of DCAP-1. The same study also reported that RNAi-mediated knockdown of genes such as lsm-1, lsm-2, and lsm-3, which are involved in the 5′ to 3′ mRNA decay steps prior to decapping, weakly reduced the accumulation of DCAP-1 in P-bodies. We found increased accumulation of ubiquitinated LSM-1 but no change in total LSM-1, LSM-2, or LSM-3 in ufd-3 KO animals compared to control. Thus, depletion of active LSM-1 may partially contribute to lower accumulation of DCAP-1 in P-bodies in ufd-3 KO animals. However, our observation of high-affinity binding between purified UFD-3 and DCAP-1 in vitro suggests that UFD-3 may be necessary to directly recruit DCAP-1 to P-bodies. It remains to be seen whether this process is a result of a change in phase separation dynamics mediated by the UFD-3 IDR.

Congruent with our observations, depletion of PLAA in HeLa cells was found to alter formation of stress granules, another type of LLPS-dependent cytoplasmic RNP granules. Stress granule formation and clearance are both modulated by VCP. A recent review examined the connection between stress granule functionality and PolyQ disorders, emphasizing how the biology of stress granules can be disrupted in the context of PolyQ diseases. UFD-3 has been shown to promote the formation of polyQ aggregates in a C. elegans model for polyQ diseases. In another study, overexpression of either VCP homologue (CDC-48.1 or CDC-48.2) partially prevented the formation of polyQ aggregation. In P-bodies, RNAi-mediated depletion of the VCP homolog cdc-48.2, the VCP cofactor genes ufd-1 or npl-4.2, or the 20S proteasome subunit genes pas-6 or pbs-2 all have the effect of increasing DCAP-1 accumulation in P-bodies. In summary, while PLAA and VCP have similar effects on stress granule formation in mammalian cells, they have opposing effects on polyQ aggregate formation and accumulation of DCAP-1 in P-bodies in C. elegans. Thus, although ubiquitin-mediated protein degradation pathways are intimately connected to the formation of cytoplasmic protein aggregates and RNP granules, PLAA may play an independent role in some of these. In support of this hypothesis, we showed that the absence of the UFD-3 IDR domain reduces DCAP-1 accumulation in P-bodies, but did not affect ubiquitin-dependent protein degradation pathways, such as PKD-2 turnover in the male tail. Collectively, these observations suggest that PLAA/UFD-3 may modulate the proteome at two distinct levels: i) protein production through posttranscriptional regulation of mRNA in P-bodies and stress granules, and ii) protein degradation through the UPS, MVB, and autophagy pathways (Fig. 5). Future work will further elucidate how these two regulatory pathways are interconnected and whether the PLAA IDR is necessary for the formation of stress granules and misfolded protein aggregates.
Methods
C. elegans Strains Generation and Maintenance.

C. elegans was maintained as described with strain N2 (Bristol) as the wild type, grown at 20 °C on NGM agar media with Escherichia coli OP50 or for some biotinylation experiments E. coli bioB (a gift from Dr. John E. Cronan) as a food source. ufd-3 knockout and deletion strains were generated by CRISPR-Cas9 genome editing and homology-directed repair, using direct injection of CRISPR-Cas9 ribonucleoprotein complexes and linear DNA oligonucleotides with short homology arms as repair templates, as described in ref.. For initial identification of positive genome-edited candidates, we used the unc-58(L466F) change as a phenotypic coconversion marker as described by Arribere et al.. ufd-3(sy1796) and ufd-3(sy1798) were generated by the insertion of a universal 43-nucleotide-long knock-in cassette (STOP-IN) within ufd-3 exons at the positions indicated in Fig. 1A, effectively disrupting translation, as described by Wang et al.. ufd-3(sy2087) was generated by deleting the entire UFD-3 protein coding region. ufd-3(sy2201) was generated by deleting the regions encoding amino acids 501-552 of the UFD-3 long isoform, which included parts of exons 5 and 6 and intron 5. See SI Appendix, Table S1 for exact sequences of the insertions and flanking regions in these alleles and for a complete list of all strains used in this study.

For proximity labeling experiments, we injected a mixture of plasmids encoding rab-3p::3xHA::TurboID::UFD-3::let-858 3′UTR (50 ng/μL), rab-3p::mCherry (pGH8, 20 ng/μL), and 1 kb DNA ladder (New England Biolabs, 25 ng/μL) into the syncytial gonads of AX7884 worms. We isolated 5 to 6 lines expressing extrachromosomal arrays based on red fluorescence in neurons. We then X-ray irradiated these lines to integrate the transgene into the genome. Following irradiation, we isolated several lines and screened for stable expression of the transgene in 100% of progeny, along with lack of any gross developmental, growth, locomotion, and fertility defects.
Growth Assay.

Day 1 adult animals (n = 5) were isolated on OP50 lawns on Petri plates containing NGM agar and allowed to lay eggs for 2 h. After 2 h the adults were removed and the plates were incubated at 20 °C. At the indicated timepoints, the plates were retrieved from the incubator, and images of the worms were collected using the WormLab Imaging System (MBF Bioscience). The experiments were repeated with two biological replicates and 2 to 3 technical replicates, to obtain images of at least 35 worms of each strain for every time point. Worm lengths were determined using the automatic worm detection and measurement tools in the proprietary WormLab software (MBF Bioscience). We used body length as a proxy for growth stages as for the strains examined in this experiment, the average body lengths between strains were comparable at specific growth stages.
Locomotion Assay.

For locomotion assays >50 well-fed mid-L4 stage hermaphrodites were picked 16 to 18 h before the start of the experiment. Assay plates were prepared by seeding standard 6 cm NGM Petri plates with a thin layer of E. coli OP50 that covered the entire surface of the agar and allowed to grow overnight at room temperature to form a thin lawn. At the start of each experiment, 5 d 1 post-L4 adult animals were picked onto an assay plate and allowed to acclimatize to the plate for 1 min. Videos of the worms were acquired on the WormLab Imaging System (MBF Bioscience) at 7.5 frames per second, for a duration of 5 min. A total of 90 worms were imaged for each strain, with two biological replicates and 8 to 10 technical replicates. Movement of the worms was tracked using the automated worm detection, tracking, and measurement tools in the proprietary WormLab software. Each worm track was manually inspected for tracking errors before analysis.
Brood Size Assay.

Single L4 stage animals (n > =20 for each strain) were isolated on OP50 lawns on Petri plates containing NGM agar. The plates were incubated at 20 °C. Every day the animals were transferred onto new plates. Worms that had crawled off the agar or were consumed by internally hatched progeny were censored. The eggs laid each day were allowed to hatch and develop for 2 to 3 d before counting.
Lifespan Assay.

10 L4 stage worms were isolated on OP50 lawns on Petri plates containing NGM agar. The adult worms were transferred to new plates every day until they stopped laying eggs. Worms were scored as alive if they moved spontaneously or upon being prodded gently with a platinum wire. Worms that had crawled off the agar or were consumed by internally hatched progeny were censored. Plates that acquired fungal or bacterial contamination were also censored. Dead worms were removed from the plate. The experiment continued until all the worms were dead.
Chemotaxis Assay.

Synchronized populations of young adult animals were washed off plates with chemotaxis buffer (25 mM NaCl, 1.5 mM Tris-base, and 3.5 mM Tris-Cl pH 7.0) and collected in microcentrifuge tubes. The worms were allowed to settle at the bottom of the tube, the supernatant was removed and the tube was filled with fresh chemotaxis buffer. This was repeated 3 times to remove as much E. coli as possible. The chemotaxis plates were prepared by pouring 16 mL of chemotaxis agar (1.5% agar, 25 mM NaCl, 1.5 mM Tris-base, and 3.5 mM Tris-Cl pH 7.0 into 6 cm petri dishes. The plates were allowed to dry uncovered in a laminar flow hood for 1 h to remove any moisture from condensation. The test and control spots were marked at 1.5 cm away from the center of the plate on opposite sides. 1 μL of 1 M sodium azide solution was added to the test and control spots. A small droplet containing (15 to 30) worms was placed at the center of the plate. As the liquid in the droplet gradually disappeared, the worms started crawling on the agar surface. At this point, 1 μL of the test (Benzaldehyde 1:200 dissolved in ethanol, Diacetyl 1:1,000 dissolved in ethanol) and control (ethanol) solutions were placed at the respective spots. The plates were immediately covered with the lids and were not disturbed for the duration of the assay (30 min). At the end of the assay, the number of worms at either spot or elsewhere in the plate was counted. Plates with too few (fewer than 15) or too many (more than 30) total worms were censored. Male Mating Behavior Assay.

We prepared mating assay plates by seeding a small droplet of OP50 at the center of 6 cm NGM agar Petri plates, to create a small lawn about ~1 cm in diameter. Just prior to starting the assay, we placed 4 gravid adult unc-119(ed3) hermaphrodites on the lawn, roughly equidistant from each other and toward the edge of the lawn. We then placed a single adult male (wild type or ufd-3 KO) at the center of the lawn and monitored its behavior. We scored the animals on whether they stopped forward movement upon encountering a hermaphrodite, performed backward scanning movement along the hermaphrodite body, and stopped upon locating the vulva. We monitored the male for up to 30 min or until it left the hermaphrodite.
Sample Preparation for Global Proteomics.

Asynchronous populations of N2, PS9498 ufd-3(sy1796) and PS9500 ufd-3(sy1798) worms were cultivated on NGM Petri plates seeded with OP50 at 20 °C for varying lengths of time until just before their food source was depleted. At the time of sample harvesting, we visually confirmed that the relative proportions of different stages of worms were similar for each strain. The worms were washed off the culture plates (3 plates for each strain) in M9 buffer and collected in microcentrifuge tubes. After the worms settled at the bottom of the tube, the supernatant was carefully removed and fresh M9 buffer was added. This washing process to remove bacteria was repeated three times. After the final wash, the supernatant was removed, and the packed worm pellet was flash-frozen in liquid nitrogen before being stored at –80 °C.

Frozen C. elegans samples were resuspended in lysis buffer (20 mM HEPES, pH 7.5; 100 mM NaCl; 0.2% DDM [n-dodecyl-β-D-maltoside]; 1× Halt Protease and Phosphatase Inhibitor Cocktail, EDTA-free (Thermo Fisher); 1 mM NEM [N-ethylmaleimide]; 20 μM MG132) by pipetting up and down five times. The samples were then transferred to tubes and sonicated at 65 A for two 15-s intervals with a 5-min pause between cycles using a Sonic Dismembrator (Model FB505, Fisher Scientific). After sonication, lysates were centrifuged at 21,300 g for 10 min. The supernatant was carefully collected, avoiding the lipid layer and protein concentration was determined using Thermo Fisher BCA kit. Lysates with 100 μg were then processed and digested using the EasyPep™ Mini MS Sample Prep Kit (Thermo Fisher Scientific), following the manufacturer’s protocol. Briefly, we aliquoted 100 μg of protein into a microcentrifuge tube and added lysis buffer to final 100 μL. We used the rest of reagents from the kit for reduction, alkylation, and LysC/Trypsin digestion overnight and then desalted the peptide. Samples were dried in a vacuum concentrator (Labconco).
Sample Preparation for Ubiquitin Enrichment Experiments.

Asynchronous populations of N2 and PS10196 (ufd-3(sy2087)) worms were cultivated on NGM plates seeded with OP50 at 20 °C for varying lengths of time until just before their food source was depleted. At the time of sample harvesting, we visually confirmed that the relative proportions of different stages of worms were similar for each strain. Then the worms were collected in microcentrifuge tubes, washed, and frozen as described in the earlier sections. For each replicate, we used enough plates to obtain about 1 mL packed volume of worms after centrifugation.

Frozen C. elegans samples were resuspended in EasyPep™ Lysis Buffer (Thermo Scientific) and transferred to tubes for sonication, following the previously described protocol. After sonication, the lysates were centrifuged at 21,300 g for 10 min, and the supernatant was carefully collected, avoiding the lipid layer. The lysates with 10 mg proteins were then processed and digested using the EasyPep™ Maxi MS Sample Prep Kit (Thermo Fisher Scientific), following the manufacturer’s protocol. Finally, 5 mg lyophilized peptides were enriched using the PTMScan® Ubiquitin Remnant Motif (K-ε-GG) Kit (Cell Signaling Technology) according to the manufacturer’s protocol.
Sample Preparation for Proximity Labeling Experiment.

Synchronized populations of AX7884 (control strain, no TurboID) and PS10308 (strain expressing neuron-specific TurboID fused to UFD-3 in the same genetic background as AX7884) were cultivated on NGM agar Petri plates seeded with E. coli OP50 or E. coli bioB (strain deficient in Biotin production, a gift from Dr. John E. Cronan). The worms were allowed to grow to L4 stage before being collected in microcentrifuge tubes, washed, and frozen as described in the earlier sections. For each replicate, we used enough plates to obtain about 1 mL packed volume of worms after centrifugation.

Frozen C. elegans samples were resuspended in EasyPep™ Lysis Buffer (Thermo Scientific) and transferred to tubes for sonication, following the previously described protocol. After sonication, the lysates were centrifuged at 21,300 g for 10 min. The supernatant was carefully collected, avoiding the lipid layer. A total of 6 mg of protein was incubated overnight at 4 °C with washed streptavidin magnetic beads (Pierce Streptavidin Magnetic Beads, Thermo Fisher Scientific) at a ratio of 6 mg protein to 400 μL beads. Following binding, the beads were washed with the following buffers in the indicated order and number of repeats, each time for 2 min: lysis buffer (2×), 1 M KCl (1×), 0.1 M Na2CO3 (1×), 2 M urea (1×), 4 M urea (1×), lysis buffer (2×), and 20 mM HEPES pH 7.5 (5×). After washing, the enriched biotinylated proteins were digested on the beads. To begin digestion, 100 μL of 8 M urea was added to gently resuspend the beads, followed by 1 μL of 500 mM TCEP [tris(2-carboxyethyl) phosphine]. The mixture was incubated at 37 °C with shaking at 750 rpm for 20 min. Subsequently, 3 μL of 500 mM CAA (2-chloroacetamide) was added and incubated at 37 °C, shaking at 750 rpm for 15 min. Next, 2 μL of Endoproteinase Lys-C (100 ng/μL) was added, and the sample was incubated at 37 °C, shaking at 750 rpm for 4 h. The sample was then diluted to 2 M urea with 375 μL of 50 mM HEPES pH 8.0, followed by the addition of 5 μL of 100 mM CaCl2. To complete digestion, 3 μL of trypsin (100 ng/μL) was added, and the sample was incubated at 37 °C with shaking at 750 rpm for 14 to 24 h. Finally, C18 spin columns (Thermo Scientific) were used to desalt the digested peptides following the manufacturer’s protocol.
Liquid Chromatography–Tandem Mass Spectrometry.

Peptides were resuspended in 10 to 15 μL of buffer (2% ACN, 0.2% formic acid). P concentration was determined using fluorescent peptide concentration kit (Thermo Fisher Scientific), LC-MS/MS analysis of the 500 to 1,000 ng peptides were performed on an EASY-nLC 1200 (Thermo Fisher Scientific) coupled to an Q Exactive HF hybrid quadrupole-Orbitrap mass spectrometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific) for global proteomics. For UFD-3 proximity labeling and ubiquitin enrichment, samples were loaded onto a Vanquish Neo UHPLC system (Thermo Fisher Scientific) with an Orbitrap Eclipse Tribrid mass spectrometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific). Peptides were separated on an Aurora UHPLC column (25 cm × 75 µm, 1.6 µm C18, AUR2-25075C18A, Ion Opticks) with a flow rate of 0.35 µL/min for a total duration of 135 or 196 min ionized at 1.6 kV in the positive ion mode. The gradient was composed of 6% solvent B (12.5 or 11 min), 6 to 25% B (82.5 or 124 min), 25 to 40% B (30 or 45 min), 40 to 98% B (1 min) and 98% B (15 min); solvent A: 2% ACN and 0.2% FA in water; solvent B: 80% ACN and 0.2% FA. For Q Exactive HF, MS1 scans were acquired at a resolution of 60,000 from 375 to 1,500 m/z, with an AGC target of 1e6, and a maximum injection time of 15 ms. In MS2 scans, 12 abundant ions were acquired at a resolution of 30,000, with an AGC target 1e5, a maximum injection time of 45 ms, and a normalized collision energy of 28. Dynamic exclusion was set to 30 s, and ions with charges +1, +7, +8, and greater than +8 were excluded. The temperature of the ion transfer tube was set to 275 °C, and the S-lens RF level was set to 60. For Eclipse, MS1 scans were acquired at the resolution of 120,000 from 375 to 2,000 m/z, AGC target 1e6, and maximum injection time 50 ms. MS2 scans were acquired in the ion trap using fast scan rate on precursors with 2 to 7 charge states and quadrupole isolation mode (isolation window: 0.7 m/z) with higher-energy collisional dissociation (HCD, 30%) activation type. Dynamic exclusion was set to 30 s. The temperature of the ion transfer tube was 300 °C and the S-lens RF level was set to 30.
Proteomic Data Analysis.

Raw data files were analyzed using Proteome Discoverer (PD) (version 3.0, Thermo Fisher Scientific) based on the CHIMERYS algorithm against the UniProt C. elegans reference proteome database (UP000001940). The maximum missed cleavages were set to 2. Dynamic modifications were set to oxidation on methionine (M, +15.995 Da) and carbamidomethylation on cysteine residues (C, +57.021 Da) was set as a fixed modification. The maximum parental mass error was set to 10 ppm, and the MS2 mass tolerance was set to 0.3 Da. The false discovery threshold was set strictly to 0.01 using the Percolator Node validated by q-value. The relative abundance of parental peptides was calculated by integration of the area under the curve of the MS1 peaks using the Minora LFQ node. The RAW data have been deposited to the ProteomeXchange Consortium via the PRIDE partner repository with the dataset identifier PXD059010 https://www.ebi.ac.uk/pride/archive/projects/PXD059010.
Bioinformatic Analysis.

Proteome Discoverer output Excel files were processed using the tidyproteomics package in R (version 4.2.2) for data tidying. The raw data without further normalization or imputation were analyzed using an empirical Bayes test based on the limma R package, using function limma::eBayes(). Volcano plots were generated using Python, based on the outputs from tidyproteomics. Gene Ontology enrichment analysis was performed according to the results obtained from tidyproteomics using the WormBase enrichment tool (https://wormbase.org/tools/enrichment/tea/tea.cgi).
DCAP-1 Localization to P-Body Assay.

A strain expressing DCAP-1::dsRed from an integrated transgene (bpIs37 [dcap-1p::dcap-1::dsRed+rol-6(su1006)]) was obtained from the Caenorhabditis Genetics Center (CGC). All mutants tested were combined into this background by genetic crosses. Animals were synchronized by picking mid-L4 stage hermaphrodites 18 h prior to imaging. Day 1 postL4 adult hermaphrodite C. elegans were picked onto microscope slides with 5% agarose pads and anesthetized using 5 mM levamisole. The slides were sealed using VALAP (1:1:1 Vaseline, Lanolin, Paraffin) sealant. Z-stack images (Z-axis range = 40 µm, Z-resolution = 1 µm) of the anterior end of the worm were acquired on a ZEISS Axio Imager Z2 using a 40× oil immersion objective. Maximum intensity projection of each image was created using Fiji. DCAP-1 fluorescence in the head region was analyzed using a custom Python script, that automatically selected a 100 × 50 pixel2 region of interest (ROI) centered around the region of maximum average fluorescence intensity in the head and calculated the average intensity in the ROI. To determine P-body number, the range of fluorescence intensity in each ROI was first normalized to the bottom and top 0.5 percentile intensity. Individual puncta were then detected in the normalized image using a 2D-peak detection algorithm from the Python “findpeaks” library, applying a static threshold.
His::UFD-3, His::DCAP-1 Construction and Purification.

The ufd-3 gene was synthesized by GeneScript, while the dcap-1 gene (clone ID: OCa344176) was obtained from GeneScript. Both genes were separately cloned into pRSFDuet and pACYCDuet vectors, each with a His-tag for purification purposes. E. coli BL21-Gold (DE3) (Agilent) served as a host for protein expression. Each E. coli transformant was cultured in Terrific Broth (TB) medium (Fisher) containing 50 μg/mL kanamycin or 50 μg/mL chloramphenicol at 37 °C and 220 rpm until the cell density reached 0.6 to 0.8 at OD600. Protein expression was induced by the addition of isopropyl-β-D-thiogalactopyranoside (IPTG) to a final concentration of 0.1 mM, followed by further incubation for 24 h at 16 °C. The cells were harvested by centrifugation at 4,300 g for 10 min, flash-frozen in liquid nitrogen, and then stored at −80 °C.

For lysis, the cell pellets were resuspended in buffer (1× PBS, 5 mM imidazole, pH 7.4) and disrupted using an LM10 Microfluidizer (Microfluidics International Corporation). Insoluble debris was removed by centrifugation at 20,000 × g for 40 min, and the resulting supernatant was subjected to purification using a Ni-NTA resin column (Qiagene). The column was washed with 10 column volumes (CVs) of lysis buffer followed by 10 CVs of wash buffer (1× PBS, 40 mM imidazole, pH 7.4). His6-tagged proteins were eluted with elution buffer (1× PBS, 250 mM imidazole, pH 7.4).

The fractions containing the target proteins, as determined by SDS-PAGE, were concentrated using Amicon® Ultra-15 Centrifugal Filter Devices (Millipore, USA) and desalted using a PD-10 Desalting Column (Cytiva, #17085101) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Protein concentrations were quantified using the Pierce™ BCA Protein Assay Kit (Thermo Scientific).

The Ni-NTA purified proteins were concentrated and filtered using Centrifugal Filters (Merck Millipore, #UFC30GV0S) by centrifugation at 10,000 × g at 4 °C for 1 min. The samples were then loaded into 96-well plates for analysis on a size exclusion chromatography (SEC) system (Cytiva). Separation was performed using a Superose 6 Increase 10/300 GL column (Cytiva) with GF buffer (20 mM HEPES, 150 mM KCl, 1 mM MgCl2, and 5% glycerol, pH 7.4) at a flow rate of 0.5 mL/min. Fractions were collected based on SDS-PAGE results, and protein concentrations were measured using the Pierce™ BCA Protein Assay Kit.

PKD-2 Localization Assay.

A strain expressing PKD-2::GFP (PT3775), in which gfp was inserted at the endogenous pkd-2 locus using CRISPR-mediated genome editing was a gift from Maureen Barr, Rutgers University, New Brunswick, NJ.
